deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from earlier sections). A wide vessel holds water to depth AB = a. A vertical tube BC of length b and cross-section gg hangs from its bottom and discharges through an orifice CC of area kk. The atmospheric pressure, expressed as a water head, is l (Euler takes about 30 ft). Euler's friction law makes the wall friction proportional to the pressure ('status compressionis') and inversely proportional to g, with a small coefficient α. This is why exponentials e^{±αb/g} appear. The efflux height is v, the head due to the exit velocity. To first order in α, the previous page gives v = a+b − (αb/g)(a + b/2 + l − (k⁴/g⁴)(a+b)). For gg = kk this reduces to v = a+b − (αb/g)(l − b/2). For b > 2l that formula would give v > a+b, i.e. friction speeding up the jet, which is absurd.

§51 resolves the paradox. Water fills the tube only so long as it is pressed against the walls. If the pressure somewhere vanishes or turns negative, the water leaves the wall and leaves a void, and the computed motion is invalid. So the calculation is legitimate only if the pressure is positive everywhere.

§52. Let R be the pressure head at the top section BB. The relation from §36 is solved for R and expanded in α. To zeroth order, R = l + a − (k⁴/g⁴)(a+b). In modern terms this is Bernoulli at B: R = l + a − (k⁴/g⁴)v with v ≈ a+b, since continuity gives the velocity head at B as (k⁴/g⁴)v.

§53. B is where the pressure is lowest. Positivity there requires l + a > (k⁴/g⁴)(a+b), i.e. b < (g⁴/k⁴)(l+a) − a. For a fully open tube (gg = kk) this means b < l: the tube cannot exceed about one atmospheric water head (about 30 ft). The case b = 2l is therefore excluded.

At the admissible maximum b = l (finished on the next page), v = a + l − αl²/(2g). This is less than the frictionless a+l, so the friction law and the positivity constraint are consistent.
errors: The printed solution for R from the §36 relation is not algebraically consistent. Solving l = R e^{-αb/g} + (g/α)(1 − e^{αb/g}) + (k⁴/g⁴)v − v gives R = e^{αb/g}[l + (g/α)(e^{αb/g} − 1) + v(1 − k⁴/g⁴)]. The printed line instead has e^{-αb/g} multiplying l and a minus sign before (g/α)(e^{αb/g} − 1). The following expansion (l + αbl/g − b − αbb/g + …) does not follow exactly from either form, so the signs in §36 or here are probably garbled. The zeroth-order result R = l + a − (k⁴/g⁴)(a+b), which is all Euler uses, is correct (it is just Bernoulli plus continuity).
The series is printed e^{αb/g} = 1 + αb/g + α²b²/g²; the quadratic term should be α²b²/(2g²). This is harmless, since only zeroth order is kept.

The underlying friction law (resistance proportional to pressure rather than to velocity) is physically wrong. The paradox v > a+b is an artifact of that law, which Euler patches with the positivity constraint rather than recognising it.

ideas.what: Validity of the flow solution requires positive pressure everywhere; where the pressure would become zero or negative the liquid separates from the wall and leaves a void.
ideas.modern_name: Cavitation / column-separation criterion (p > 0, or p > vapour pressure)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1750s papers on pipe flow and turbines), with antecedents in Daniel Bernoulli's Hydrodynamica (1738)
ideas.where_published: Euler's earlier pipe-flow memoir 'Sur le mouvement de l'eau par des tuyaux de conduite' (Berlin Mém., 1750s) also discusses separation at negative pressure; exact E-number unsure

ideas.what: Maximum length of a vertical open discharge pipe is about one atmospheric water head (b < l), with the general bound b < (g⁴/k⁴)(l+a) − a for a contracted outlet.
ideas.modern_name: Barometric limit on draft-tube / downpipe length (Bernoulli plus a positivity constraint)
ideas.where_published: Possibly in Euler's pipe-flow memoirs; unsure

ideas.what: Using a physical admissibility constraint to discard an absurd prediction (friction accelerating the jet) of an approximate friction model.
ideas.modern_name: Consistency check of a constitutive law

deep.surprise_reason: The page applies Bernoulli's equation plus the positivity-of-pressure (cavitation) criterion, which Euler had already stated in his 1750s hydraulics. The bound b < l for a downpipe is standard. Nothing appears to be absent from the record, and the pressure-proportional friction law it rests on is a known dead end discussed in histories of fluid mechanics.
transcription_corrections: The series term printed as α²b²/g² matches the image, but it is a misprint for α²b²/(2g²).
§53 'b<l' may be printed with an extra stroke ('b ⋜ l' or similar) in the image; the sense is b < l.
